perspective:
From Mason Hurley’s accessible perspective:

- I am an accountant at a small community center. Martha Moua is a personal care aide there and my colleague. We are professional but not personally close; we interact mainly about work.
- I reviewed the community center’s financial reports and noticed discrepancies: healthcare expenses seemed unusually high and did not match usual spending patterns. This made me suspicious and anxious that Martha might be mismanaging funds.
- I asked Martha to discuss the recent financial report and pointed out those high healthcare numbers. She said there was likely a reasonable explanation and asked which discrepancies I meant. After looking, she said there might have been a misentry and that she would review and correct any errors.
- After reviewing the report with Martha, I concluded the discrepancies were a clerical error, not mismanagement. I felt relieved but embarrassed. I thanked her for clarifying and apologized for my initial suspicion. She said errors happen, was glad it was cleared up, understood I was being thorough, and suggested double-checking entries next time.
- I then believed Martha was competent, but that the current financial management system was inadequate. I felt frustrated with the system and empathetic toward Martha. I told her the issue was not her management but the system, and I proposed a new, more robust financial system. I said I would draft a proposal and wanted her input. She agreed, asked what I suggested, offered to help, and said it should address the gaps we identified.
- I finished drafting the proposal. I hoped it would benefit operations but was uncertain whether management would approve or implement it. Martha told me it was solid, encouraged me to present it confidently because the benefits were clear, and agreed to help gather data. I planned to prepare a detailed presentation.
- I presented the proposal to management. I felt satisfied with my effort but physically and mentally exhausted, believing I had done everything possible and that the decision was now up to management. I told Martha the presentation went well and that I planned to take a few days off to recharge. She praised my work, said I deserved a break, and offered help while I was away.

I do not yet know management’s final decision or any private reasons behind their response.
